source: Norman (1981) Categorization of action slips
finding: Norman built an action-schema theory. An intention activates a parent schema and child schemas. Each schema has an activation value and trigger conditions. Slips arise when this system activates or triggers the wrong schema.
numbers: Three slip classes: (a) errors in forming the intention (mode errors, description errors); (b) faulty activation (capture, data-driven and associative activation, loss of intention, misordering); (c) faulty triggering (spoonerisms, blends, intrusions of thoughts, premature triggering). About 1,000 incidents examined, about 200 from Norman's own collection.
limits: Corpus is collected anecdotes, not counted rates. Norman notes that catch information was often not recorded.
agent_relevance: Slips and mistakes need different defences. A scaffold can cut slips by checking outputs. It cannot cut wrong intentions that way.

source: Norman (1981), the detection of slips section
finding: Norman argued slips need a feedback mechanism. A slip is caught only if the monitor is made aware of a gap between intention and act. Many slips are caught by the doer early. Some are never caught. Omission slips (forgot to do something) are hardest to detect because nothing signals them.
numbers: Table 3 gives examples of slips caught at stages from 'in the act' to long after. One reported slip (orange juice poured in the mug) was found only when later pouring coffee.
quote: For a slip to be detected, the monitoring mechanism must be made aware of the discrepancy between intention and act
limits: No detection rate given. Norman writes that in most slip collections the catch information is not recorded.
agent_relevance: Detection needs a visible gap between intent and act. Our agent should write intent and expected result before acting, so code can compute the gap (supports G2).

source: Reason (1990) Human Error (Cambridge University Press)
finding: Reason's GEMS model builds on Rasmussen's skill, rule and knowledge levels. Slips and lapses are failures of execution or storage. Mistakes are failures of planning, rule-based or knowledge-based. Reason also names violations and latent conditions.
numbers: Recalled, not read: Reason's earlier diary study (1979) had 35 people log slips for two weeks, 433 slips; storage failures were the largest class (about 40%). Verify before citing.
limits: Book not opened this session. Numbers from memory. The framework is cited here through Blavier et al. (2005), which was opened.
agent_relevance: The slip / lapse / mistake split maps to different repair routes: re-execute, re-prompt memory, or re-plan.

source: Blavier, Rouy, Nyssen, de Keyser (2005) Prospective issues for error detection, Ergonomics 48(7)
finding: A review of the error-handling chain: detection, then identification, then recovery. Sellen and Norman treat these as three separable steps. One can detect without identifying, and identify without recovering.
numbers: Reason (1990) lists three detection routes: self-monitoring, the environment (forcing functions), and another person. Doireau et al. (1997), as quoted by the review: self-detected errors were recovered in about 90% of cases; detection by a third person was rarer (about 30%).
quote: Error detection is the realization that an error has occurred independently from knowing what the error is like
limits: Secondary source. Numbers are as quoted by the review from a French-language study that was not opened.
agent_relevance: Our loop has the same three steps: detect (code check), identify (cite the failing output, G2), recover (revise). Keep them as separate states.

source: Blavier et al. (2005), citing Woods (1984) and Nyssen (1997) on diagnosis errors
finding: Slips (execution errors) are easy for operators to self-detect. Diagnosis errors usually need an outsider, a 'new mind'. Operators fixate on their own picture of the system state, which blocks detection.
numbers: Doireau et al. (1997), as noted by the review: outsiders detect better if they are domain experts, if the error is a mistake not a slip, and if detection is close in time to the error.
limits: Qualitative as reported. Woods 1984 and Nyssen 1997 not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports G4 and G2: the same model re-reading its own diagnosis is the fixated operator. An independent check (code, different input, held-out case) plays the new mind.

source: Blavier et al. (2005), citing Sellen (1994) and Sellen and Norman (1992)
finding: Sellen's taxonomy of detection: action-based (plan vs executed action, intention vs action), outcome-based (expected vs actual outcome; match with known own error forms), and limiting functions (a physical block). Slips are mostly caught through the action. Mistakes are caught only through the outcome, a limiting function, or another person, because a mistaken plan does not conflict with the action.
numbers: Taxonomy built on a diary corpus of nearly 600 errors (Sellen 1994). Internal mismatch can only pick out slips.
limits: Review summary. Allwood's four episode types (affirmative evaluation, standard check, direct error hypothesis, error suspicion) are behavioural, not cognitive mechanisms (Sellen's critique).
agent_relevance: A plan-level mistake gives no internal alarm. Only an outcome check against something the plan was not fitted to can reveal it. This is G3.

source: Sellen (1994) Detection of everyday errors, Applied Psychology 43(4):475-498
finding: Diary study of everyday slips and mistakes. It proposes how errors are detected: action-based, outcome-based, and through limiting functions. It also covers why detection fails.
numbers: Corpus: nearly 600 slips and mistakes. Three detection categories.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session. No full text, so no per-category percentages are recorded here.
agent_relevance: Design the loop so detection has three sources: action trace, outcome check, hard limits (tests, type checks).

source: Allwood (1984) Error detection processes in statistical problem solving, Cognitive Science 8(4)
finding: Think-aloud study of statistical problem solving. Evaluation episodes fell into four types. Better solvers caught more of their own errors, mostly through spontaneous detection triggers.
numbers: 16 participants, two statistical problems (from a search summary, not the paper). Allwood and Montgomery (1982) had 10 participants; one detection type appeared only when told to check after each substep.
limits: Abstract-level knowledge only. The paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Prompted checks change what is found (instructed checks differ from spontaneous ones). Supports G1: doubt on a signal, not on a timer.

source: Rasmussen (1983) Skills, rules and knowledge; signals, signs and symbols, IEEE SMC-13
finding: Rasmussen's SRK framework: behaviour runs at skill, rule or knowledge level. Error types differ by level. Knowledge-based errors arise in unfamiliar situations with no stored rule.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened this session; described from memory and via Blavier (2005).
agent_relevance: Our S-states can map to SRK: routine retrieval (skill), known operator (rule), novel problem (knowledge). Mistake risk is highest in the last.

source: Hollnagel (1998) Cognitive Reliability and Error Analysis Method, CREAM (Elsevier)
finding: CREAM separates genotypes (causes) from phenotypes (observable error modes). It uses four cognitive functions: observation, interpretation, planning, execution. Context acts through nine common performance conditions and four control modes: scrambled, opportunistic, tactical, strategic.
numbers: Recalled, not read: failure probability intervals per control mode roughly strategic 0.00005-0.01, tactical 0.001-0.1, opportunistic 0.01-0.5, scrambled 0.1-1.0. Verify before citing.
limits: Book not opened. Numbers from memory. Hollnagel treats error as a result of context, not a stable trait.
agent_relevance: An agent has the same four functions: read the input, interpret, plan, execute. We can log failures by function. A CREAM-style control mode could be set by code (time left, checks passed).

source: Reason (2000) Human error: models and management, BMJ 320:768-770
finding: Person approach blames individuals. System approach assumes people are fallible and asks how defences failed. Swiss-cheese model: layered defences each with holes from active failures and latent conditions. Accidents happen when holes line up.
numbers: About 90% of aviation maintenance quality lapses were judged blameless. Names three high-reliability organisation types (nuclear carriers, nuclear plants, air traffic control).
quote: We cannot change the human condition, but we can change the conditions under which humans work
limits: Page read through a fetch tool that summarises the text, so figures come from that summary. Opinion and review, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on one check layer. Stack independent layers (test, held-out case, mutated input) and expect each to leak.

source: Williams (1986) HEART, as described on Wikipedia
finding: HEART gives a nominal error probability for a task type, then multiplies it by error-producing-condition factors. Each condition can only worsen performance.
numbers: Worked example: nominal 0.003 with five conditions gives a final estimate of about 0.27.
limits: Secondary page. It says the condition data were never fully published and that conditions are assumed independent, which is often false. Kirwan's validation found reasonable but not clearly better accuracy.
agent_relevance: Human reliability numbers are expert-judged, not measured. Do not import human error rates as priors for an LLM agent. Measure our own.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet, ICLR
finding: With oracle labels telling when to stop, self-correction looks good. Without labels (intrinsic self-correction) accuracy falls on all tested benchmarks. Earlier gains came from using ground truth to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4 with oracle: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: Tests GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2. HotpotQA sample only 100. The oracle setting is not a real use case.
agent_relevance: G2 evidence: the model alone cannot tell good answers from bad. Revise only on code-found failure.

source: Huang et al. (2024), intrinsic self-correction tables
finding: Each extra round of intrinsic self-correction lowered accuracy. On CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 changed correct answers to wrong ones often, because wrong options look relevant.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 (1 call) to 75.1 (3 calls) to 74.7 (5 calls); CSQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Depends on the generic self-correction prompt. The authors tried several other prompts (their Tables 5 and 6) and all lost accuracy.
agent_relevance: A forced 'are you sure?' step can cost accuracy. Matches our own word-puzzle result (92% plain vs 75% with forced doubt).

source: Huang et al. (2024), multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at an equal number of responses.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: standard single prompt 76.7. Self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2. Debate round 1 (6 responses) 83.2, round 2 (9 responses) 83.0.
limits: GPT-3.5 only for this table.
agent_relevance: Gains from 'debate' are mostly the extra samples. Counting votes in code is the cheaper tool (G5).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error, Findings of ACL
finding: They built BIG-Bench Mistake: chain-of-thought traces from PaLM 2 with a human-marked first logical mistake. Five LLMs are poor at finding the mistake. If the mistake step is given, backtracking and regenerating from it fixes many traces.
numbers: 5 tasks, 300 traces per task (255 incorrect, 45 correct). GPT-4 best, overall mistake-location accuracy 52.87 with direct step-level prompting. Tracking shuffled objects (5.4 steps on average): GPT-4 62.29 (direct trace), 65.33 (direct step), 90.67 (CoT step); GPT-3.5-Turbo 10.10, 1.67, 19.00.
quote: the main bottleneck in self-correction methods is the identification of mistakes, rather than the correction process
limits: Traces come from one model (PaLM 2). Only 45 correct traces per task, so the effect on correct answers is poorly estimated.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is locating the error, not repairing it. Code should locate (G2): run tests, compare with the spec, then hand the located failure to the model.

source: Tyen et al. (2024), backtracking with oracle vs random location
finding: Backtracking with the true mistake location raised accuracy on wrong traces by 18 to 44 points and cost 0 to 11 points on right traces. A random location gave smaller gains and bigger losses.
numbers: Oracle location: gains +18.04 to +43.92, losses 0.00 to -11.43 (points). Random location: gains +5.16 to +21.57, losses -6.67 to -15.91. A trained classifier at about 60-70% mistake-finding accuracy was enough for gains to beat losses.
limits: Oracle labels are rarely available. Net gain depends on base accuracy: at 99% base accuracy the net could be negative (their worked example 99% to 92.8%).
agent_relevance: Make the loop proportional to the fail rate: when first-pass accuracy is high, leave answers alone unless a check fails (G1).

source: Tyen et al. (2024), prompting methods trade-off
finding: Step-by-step CoT checking lowers accuracy on traces that were correct, because the checker finds mistakes that are not there. Trace-level Yes/No prompts keep correct traces but miss errors.
numbers: Direct trace-level, direct step-level and CoT step-level prompts were compared on 5 tasks and 5 models. Accuracy on no-mistake traces goes down considerably from trace-level to CoT step-level (their Figure 1).
limits: Exact per-cell numbers not recorded here. Small correct subset.
agent_relevance: Both false alarms and misses cost. Prefer code checks with known false-alarm rates.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey, TACL
finding: Critical survey of self-correction work up to May 2024. No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM in general tasks. It works where reliable external feedback exists. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: No pooled effect size. The survey gives a checklist for fair experiments and flags unfair setups: oracle labels, weak initial prompts, impractical frameworks.
limits: Survey, not new data. Covers papers up to May 2024; later work is only briefly mentioned.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and for the rule that code supplies the feedback.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: identifying process errors in mathematical reasoning (Qwen team)
finding: ProcessBench has 3,400 competition and Olympiad math cases with a human-marked earliest error step. Prompted general models used as critics beat existing process reward models on hard problems. Reasoning-specialised models critique best.
numbers: Overall F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9, best open model QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5 (figure 1). F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on erroneous and on correct samples.
limits: Math only. Models graded other models' solutions, not necessarily their own.
agent_relevance: Critique ability rises with reasoning training. A stronger, separate checker is more useful than self-review by the generator.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) Evaluating LLMs at detecting errors in LLM responses (ReaLMistake), COLM
finding: ReaLMistake has expert-labelled real errors in GPT-4 and Llama 2 70B responses across four error types. 12 LLMs detect errors at very low recall. Explanations are unreliable. Self-consistency and majority vote do not help detection.
numbers: Human annotation agreement F1 95.7. Many LLM detectors score below a random baseline in F1. Stronger models (higher LMSYS Elo) have higher precision but lower recall. Recall shifted by 16.9 +/- 20.3 points on average between two prompt wordings.
limits: Tasks are short generation tasks with GPT-4 and Llama 2 errors. Human baseline is on 35 cases per setting.
agent_relevance: G4: voting does not fix detection. Treat an LLM saying 'no error found' as weak evidence.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot, COLM 2026
finding: The same injected error is fixed when shown as the user's error but missed when shown as the model's own earlier output. The ability exists but is not used on own text.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: 64.5% average blind spot. Fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces cut the blind spot by 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cut it by 89.3%.
limits: Mostly injected errors, with a smaller test on natural errors. Mostly math, plus logic and tracking tasks. Single author.
agent_relevance: The own-output blind spot is the LLM version of the fixated operator (Woods). Present the output as someone else's, or use a separate pass, when a check is needed.

source: Tsui (2026), 'Wait' and reasoning models
finding: Reasoning models show a small or even negative blind spot. Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model nearly matches the matching reasoning model.
numbers: Macro mean accuracy, base / with Wait / reasoning model: DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 / 0.902 / 0.908; phi-4 0.325 / 0.701 / 0.707; Qwen3-14B 0.117 / 0.868 / 0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045 / 0.793 / 0.894.
limits: Shown on tests with an injected error. Not shown for tasks with no error, where 'Wait' could cause a false alarm.
agent_relevance: A 'Wait' cue is a cheap prompt for reviewing own text. Under G1, use it only after a failed check.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning (SCoRe)
finding: Plain SFT and STaR do not make a model self-correct on its own data; they change correct answers to wrong ones. Two-stage RL (SCoRe) gives the first clearly positive self-correction gain.
numbers: MATH, Gemini 1.5 Flash: base 52.6% first try, 41.4% second try (-11.2); Self-Refine 52.8 to 51.8; SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4 (+4.4). Correct-to-wrong rate 15.8% base, 1.4% SCoRe. Wrong-to-right 9.5% base, 14.5% SCoRe. MBPP-R: 47.3% to 60.6%.
limits: Requires training. Gain is modest, one model family.
agent_relevance: Training can fix it; a scaffold cannot. So the scaffold must supply the signal from outside.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: Self-Refine helps most on tasks scored by preference or style. On math it did not help, because the model says everything looks good.
numbers: Math reasoning, GPT-3.5: 64.1 to 64.1 (0). ChatGPT feedback said 'everything looks good' in 94% of math instances. Gains of 5%+ appear when an external source tells which answers are wrong. GPT-4 dialogue preference 25.4% to 74.6%.
limits: Style-task gains are judged by models, which may favour their own text.
agent_relevance: Self-feedback misses real errors: 94% 'looks good'. This is detection failure at the root.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing, ICLR
finding: CRITIC lets the model verify with tools (search, code) and then revise. Tool feedback gives the gain. Without the tool, the revise step does little.
numbers: Text-Davinci-003 HotpotQA EM/F1: CoT 33.7/46.1; CRITIC 38.7/50.5; CRITIC without tool 34.9/46.1; oracle CRITIC 43.1/54.5. AmbigNQ EM: CoT 44.2, CRITIC 50.0, without tool 42.0.
limits: Gains are a few points on QA. Search results are cached for fairness, which hides live-web variance.
agent_relevance: Confirms G2: real output from a tool, not the model's opinion, drives the repair.

source: Lin et al. (2024) CriticBench: benchmarking LLMs for critique-correct reasoning
finding: CriticBench covers 15 datasets and 17 LLMs for generation, critique and correction. Critique skill rises linearly with generation skill. Critique output is very sensitive to the prompt.
numbers: Vicuna-13b flagged 22.04% of responses as wrong with a direct-answer critique prompt but only 4.8% with a CoT prompt, against an actual error rate of 51.63%.
limits: Critique prompts are single-shot. Oracle-feedback correction helps but in some tasks still falls short of generating from scratch.
agent_relevance: A critic that flags 5-22% when 52% are wrong is a weak alarm. Do not use an LLM critique pass as the detector.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three groups, from 1,600+ annotated traces over 7 frameworks. Verification failures (premature termination, no or incomplete verification, incorrect verification) form one group.
numbers: Inter-annotator kappa 0.88 on 150 development traces. Group shares: system design issues 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%.
limits: Describes failures of agent systems, not a controlled test of detection. Large-scale labelling used an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Verification failures are a distinct error class in agents. A CREAM-style genotype/phenotype log of our runs can start from these modes.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which agent causes task failures and when? Who&When
finding: Automated failure attribution in LLM multi-agent logs is poor. Finding the agent is easier than finding the decisive step.
numbers: Who&When has failure logs from 127 multi-agent systems. Best method: 53.5% accuracy for the responsible agent, 14.2% for the failure step. Some methods are below random. o1 and R1 also fell short.
limits: Logs are long. Methods are LLM prompts, not trained locators.
agent_relevance: Locating the first wrong step in a long agent trace is hard for a model. Keep traces short and have code log checkpoints so the failing step is known.

source: Xiao et al. (2024) KRAIL: knowledge-driven human reliability analysis with IDHEAS and LLMs
finding: LLMs plus a knowledge graph are used to estimate base human error probability under partial information. This is an LLM used inside classical human reliability analysis.
numbers: Numbers not recorded: only the abstract and first pages were skimmed.
limits: It is a nuclear human reliability tool. It estimates how humans fail, not how LLMs fail.
agent_relevance: Not directly useful to the schema. Shows CREAM/IDHEAS-style analysis is now being run with LLMs.
